rules.use_when: The reader asks how a total changed over a run of years and what it was made of, such as how many homes were finished each year and in what kind of building.

use_instead.when: There are more than four parts
The parts’ shares matter more than the total
One year’s parts are the question
The total alone tells the story

correct.caption: What kinds of homes were finished each year?

rules.title: Use a stacked area of shares to follow a whole’s mix over many years.
rule: Stack up to four parts as shares of each year’s total, from 0 to 100 percent, in the categorical inks in their order with Stone hatched (Rule 14.5). Name each band inside it at its right end and print its last share past the edge. Say in a note when a part starts or stops, such as a program that began partway through the window.

text: Shares that add to 100 every year let a reader see one part grow at another’s expense across decades. Only the baseline and the line at 100 are straight, so the bands between them are read by their thickness, which is why each one is named where it ends and its last share is printed.

rules.builders: Form stacked-area: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s46; encode.parts lists the columns from the bottom, and labels.offset draws shares (expand) or amounts (zero).
rules.use_when: The reader asks how the mix of a whole has shifted over a long run of years, such as who pays the nation’s health care bill, and the total’s size is a separate question.

use_instead.when: The run is short enough to draw a column a year
The parts’ amounts matter more than their shares
There are more than four parts

correct.caption: Who pays the nation’s health care bill?

rules.title: Use a treemap for a budget with many parts in one year.
rule: Draw each part as a rectangle whose area is its amount, largest first, every tile in light gray with a thin darker edge and a gap of the page color between tiles, and print each tile’s name, amount and share inside it. The part the title names takes the subject ink with its words in the light ink, since a tile in red would pass Rule 05.1’s 5 percent of the drawing (Rule 14.6). Fold the parts too small to hold their words at the narrowest drawing into one tile laid out last, list each in the table, and say what a negative line the treemap cannot draw leaves out.

text: Area shows the whole and each part’s weight in it at once, and the largest parts claim the most room as they claim the most money. Areas are harder to compare exactly than lengths, so every tile prints its amount and share.

rules.builders: Form treemap: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s47; labels.fold “fit” folds the fewest smallest parts that let every tile hold its words at 256 px (labels.fold_below sets a share instead), labels.fold_label names the folded tile, with {n} for its count of parts, and labels.named the tile the title names.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where the money in one budget went, the parts number more than a bar chart reads quickly, and the largest few carry the answer.

use_instead.when: The reader compares parts across years
The parts are few or must be ranked exactly
Lines add and take away on the way to a result

correct.caption: Where did federal spending go in fiscal 2026?

rules.title: Use a parliament chart for the seats in a chamber.
rule: Draw every seat as one dot on a half circle of rows, every party in the one party-mark ink, with each party’s block named with its count and set apart from the next by a narrow gap (Rule 14.7). Lay Democrats from the left, as the chart for Rule 14.28 orders the parties, Republicans from the right, and independents and vacancies between them, set apart from both blocks and each named with its own leader, so every chamber we draw reads the same way. Draw an empty seat as an open ring, and mark the seat that makes a majority with a tick. Print the date of the count, since seats change with every vacancy.

text: A dot for each seat shows a chamber as readers know it, and blocks of one ink keep color from standing for a party. The names, counts and order carry the sides, and the majority tick shows how close the largest block comes to control.

rules.builders: Form parliament: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s48; labels.order sets the blocks from left to right, labels.words their names, labels.open the group drawn as open rings and labels.majority the tick.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a chamber divides today, and the size of each block against a majority is the point.

use_instead.when: The reader compares the division across many sessions
The reader compares two or three totals
The items are things other than seats, counted one by one

correct.caption: How are the House’s seats divided by party today?

rules.title: Use a pie only for two or three parts of one whole, with each share printed.
rule: Use a pie, a reference form, when one whole splits into two or three parts and the reader needs only a rough sense of each part’s share. Start the largest slice at the top and run clockwise, name each slice with its share printed beside it, and keep the slices flat and in the inks of Rule 14.5. A slice the title names takes the subject ink, since a slice in red would pass Rule 05.1’s 5 percent of the drawing (Rule 14.6). Past three parts, or where the shares sit close together, draw bars.

text: Readers judge a slice by its angle and its area, which they read less exactly than a length. Two or three slices with their shares printed are still quick to read, and the printed figures carry the exact values.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a pie only as a sketch beside its printed shares; for a chart, build percent-bar or ranked-bar.
rules.sketch_alt: A pie of one illustrative whole in three parts, each slice named with its share printed beside it, the largest starting at the top. The shares add to 100 percent.
rules.use_when: The reader asks roughly how one whole divides, the parts are two or three, and the shares differ enough to see.

use_instead.when: The parts number four or more, or their shares sit close together
Several wholes are compared part by part
One share is the point and a single number says it

correct.caption: A pie of one illustrative whole in three parts, each slice named with its share printed beside it, the largest starting at the top.
correct.label: Pie, a sketch

rules.title: Use a donut with a number in its center only when that one number is the point.
rule: Use a donut, a reference form, for one share of a whole that a reader should remember, printed large in the center with its words under it. Give the share the subject ink, since a ring in red would pass Rule 05.1’s 5 percent of the drawing (Rule 14.6), and the rest of the ring light gray; keep the ring to two parts, and print the whole the share is of.

text: The number in the center carries the answer, and the ring shows at a glance that it is part of a whole. A ring of more than two parts asks the reader to compare arcs, which they read even less exactly than slices.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a donut only as a sketch; for a figure with its context, build big-number.
rules.sketch_alt: A donut of one illustrative whole in two parts, with the larger part’s share, 64 percent, printed in its center and the ring split at that share. The rest of the ring is gray.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what share of a whole one part holds, and a single figure answers it.

use_instead.when: The figure needs context more than a ring, such as a range or a comparison
The whole splits into three parts
The figure is a count toward a threshold

correct.caption: A donut of one illustrative whole in two parts, with the larger part’s share, 64 percent, printed in its center and the ring split at that share.
correct.label: Donut with a center number, a sketch

rules.title: Use a marimekko when the groups differ in size and each splits into the same parts.
rule: Use a marimekko, a reference form, to show two ways of dividing one whole at once: each column is as wide as its group’s share of the whole, and each column splits by the same parts as a 100 percent bar does. Name every column and part, and print each column’s width as a share, since width is the measure a reader cannot read from a scale. A cell the title names takes the subject ink, since a cell in red would pass Rule 05.1’s 5 percent of the drawing (Rule 14.6).

text: Each cell’s area is its share of the whole, so a large group’s small part can outweigh a small group’s large one, which a 100 percent bar hides. Widths and heights both carry values, so the chart asks more of the reader and needs every share printed.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a marimekko only as a sketch until a story needs one; build percent-bar for the mix within groups.
rules.sketch_alt: A marimekko of three illustrative groups, each column as wide as its group’s share of the whole and split by the shares of two answers, so each cell’s area is its share of everyone. The widest group holds half of the whole.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a whole divides by two things at once, such as who answered each way within groups of very different size, and the area of each cell is the count that matters.

use_instead.when: Only the mix within each group matters
The reader compares a few groups on one measure
The cells’ counts are the point and a table reads faster

correct.caption: A marimekko of three illustrative groups, each column as wide as its group’s share of the whole and split by the shares of two answers, so each cell’s area is its share of everyone.
correct.label: Marimekko, a sketch

rules.title: Avoid 3D pies and bars, whose depth bends every value.
rule: Leave 3D pies, 3D bars and every chart drawn with depth or tilt out of every Oath & Action piece. Draw the same values flat, as bars from one zero line, so each value is read as a length.

text: Tilting a pie stretches the near slices and shrinks the far ones, so equal shares look unequal, and the sides of a 3D bar add ink that hides where its top is. Neither adds a value the flat chart lacks.

rules.builders: No form: the kit draws nothing in 3D. The sketch, work/build/guide/specimens/s-14-57-sketch.html, draws a tilted pie beside flat bars of the same values; build the better choice with ranked-bar or percent-bar.
rules.sketch_alt: A tilted 3D pie draws two equal illustrative shares so the nearer one looks larger, and flat bars of the same values show them as equal lengths. The pie’s depth adds ink and no value.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how parts compare gets a truer answer from flat bars or a flat 100 percent bar.

use_instead.when: The reader compares a handful of values
The values are shares of one whole

correct.caption: A tilted 3D pie draws two equal illustrative shares so the nearer one looks larger, and flat bars of the same values show them as equal lengths.
correct.label: 3D pie or bar, a form that misleads

rules.title: Use a histogram to show how one measure spreads across many units.
rule: Count the units in bins of equal width and draw one column a bin, side by side with a hairline between them, from zero. Print each count over its column where it fits, and mark the median as a dashed line in the text’s ink with its own label (Rule 14.6). Choose the bins once, before drawing, and say in a note that each unit counts once; where a story turns on dates, check that no bin edge falls on an inauguration day (Rule 14.10).
A chart of thousands of units draws from a table of its bins, so the table under the chart lists the bins, each with its count, and the page stays light.

text: A histogram turns a long list into a shape a reader can see at once: where most units sit, how far the tail runs and whether there are two humps. Equal bins keep every column comparable, and the median line gives the middle without the reader adding counts.

rules.builders: Form histogram: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s49; encode start, end and count from a bin table; labels.marker draws the median line with its words, labels.x_axis and labels.y_axis name the axes.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how long, how much or how many across hundreds or thousands of people, places or records, and the shape of the spread is the answer.

use_instead.when: Each unit must stay visible and the units number fewer than about a hundred
The reader compares the spread of a few groups
Two years or two groups of the same measure need one picture

correct.caption: How long have today’s federal judges served?

rules.title: Show every item as a dot on one scale when each one should stay visible.
rule: Place each item as one dot on a single value scale, packed up and down from a center line so no dot hides another; the packing follows the data alone, so it draws the same every time. Name the items the title names with their values, in the view’s red point, or in the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for a state. Keep the rest in the light fill, and draw a total or national figure as a dashed line in the text’s ink with its own label (Rule 14.6).
A strip plot is the same form with the dots in one row; use it when the items rarely touch.

text: Every dot is an item the reader can find, so the chart shows the spread and keeps the individual places in it. Packing the dots by value alone means two builds of the same data draw the same picture, and the table under the chart gives each item’s value.

rules.builders: Form beeswarm: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s50; labels.named names the items in ink, labels.reference draws the dashed total line with labels.reference_label.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how about 20 to 100 places compare on one measure, and both the spread and a few named places matter.

use_instead.when: The items number in the hundreds or more
The reader needs each item’s exact rank and value in order
Several groups of items share the scale and the reader compares groups

correct.caption: How much does each state collect in taxes per resident?

rules.title: Use a box plot to compare the spread of a few groups.
rule: Draw one row a group, its name and count of units flush left: a box from the first to the third quartile, the values a quarter and three quarters of the way up the ranked units, so the box holds the middle half; a 2 px line at the median, the middle unit; whiskers to the last unit within one and a half times the box’s length, and each unit beyond them as a small open circle. Print each median, give the group the title names the view’s red point while that red stays within 5 percent of the drawing at every width (Rule 05.1), or the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for a region of states, and say in the measure line what the box and whiskers span.
The chart draws from a table of each group’s quartiles, median and whiskers and a table of the units past the whiskers, so a chart of thousands of units stays light.

text: Five numbers a group, the two quartiles, the median and the whiskers’ two ends, let a reader compare many units across groups at a glance. The rule for the whiskers is fixed and stated, so an open circle past them always means the same thing, and no group’s spread depends on how the chart was drawn.

rules.builders: Form box-plot: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s51; encode the five numbers and count; labels.outliers names the second dataset of units past the whiskers, labels.named the group in ink.
rules.use_when: A reader who knows the form asks how widely a measure varies within each of a few groups, such as regions, and where the middle of each group sits.

use_instead.when: One group, and its shape matters more than its quartiles
Two groups or two years, and the reader compares their whole shapes
Each unit in a small group must stay visible

correct.caption: How widely do uninsured rates vary among counties in each region?

rules.title: Overlay two distributions as stepped outlines on the same bins.
rule: Draw each year or group as a stepped outline over one baseline, with no fill, so each shape shows through the other. The series the title follows takes the subject ink at the subject weight and the other the context ink at the field weight, each named where its outline peaks. Use the same bins for both and count each unit once in each year or group.

text: Two filled histograms hide each other where they overlap, and side-by-side columns halve every bin. Outlines on shared bins let the reader see at once whether the mass moved left or right, which is the question a shift asks.

rules.builders: Form line-histogram: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s52; encode start, end, value and series from a long bin table; labels.lit names the series in ink.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether a whole distribution moved between two years, or differs between two groups, on one measure.

use_instead.when: One year or group alone
Three or more groups, each with its own spread
The reader follows a few named units from one year to the next

correct.caption: Did county child poverty rates shift between 2019 and the latest year?

rules.title: Show a population’s age and sex in a pyramid, one bar a year of age.
rule: Draw one thin bar a year of age on each side, men to the left and women to the right on one scale, the youngest at the bottom and ages labeled down the center. Both sides take one ink, and position and the names over each half carry sex. A band of ages the title names takes the view’s red as one job (Rule 14.6) while that red stays within 5 percent of the drawing at every width (Rule 05.1), and the subject ink where the red would pass that share, as ages 55 to 64 do here. Every other age takes the light fill. Set the band’s words in the empty corner and name the band by its ages, since its ink changes with the ground and in forced colors.

text: Single years show the echoes of booms and slumps in births that five-year groups smooth away, and a mirrored scale lets the reader compare men and women at every age by length alone. One ink for both sides keeps color free for the band the story names.

rules.builders: Form population-pyramid: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s53; labels.left and labels.right name the two sides, labels.point (red) or labels.named (the subject ink) a range of ages, labels.band_words its words.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how many people are at or near a given age, such as the ages of retirement programs, or how a population’s ages are shaped.

use_instead.when: The reader compares a few broad age groups
The reader follows one age group’s count over years
Two populations’ age shapes need one picture

correct.caption: How many people are near the ages of Social Security and Medicare?

rules.title: Use a violin only for experts, with its box plot drawn inside it.
rule: Use a violin, a reference form, where a technical audience compares the shapes of several distributions. Draw each group’s smoothed density as a shape mirrored about its center line, with the quartiles and median inside it, and say how the shape was smoothed. Oath & Action draws one only in a methods note or a report for specialists.

text: A violin shows a second hump that a box plot hides, but its width comes from a smoothing choice the reader cannot see. Keeping the box inside it gives every reader the quartiles they can trust.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a violin only in a specialist piece, from a density the analyst states, with the quartile box inside it as box-plot draws one.
rules.sketch_alt: Three violins, each a mirrored density shape with its quartile box and median inside, side by side on one scale; the middle group has two humps that a box plot alone would hide.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks whether a group’s values bunch in one place or two, and the quartiles alone would hide a second hump.

use_instead.when: A general reader compares the spread of a few groups
One group’s shape, with counts a reader can check

correct.caption: Three violins, each a mirrored density shape with its quartile box and median inside, side by side on one scale; the middle group has two humps that a box plot alone would hide.
correct.label: Violin, a sketch

rules.title: Stack several distributions as a ridgeline only when their order tells the story.
rule: Use a ridgeline, a reference form, for many distributions of one measure in a meaningful order, such as years: each a filled curve on its own baseline, the baselines evenly spaced and the curves allowed to overlap the row above. Name each row at its left, keep one scale for every curve, and draw the subject in ink with the rest light.

text: Overlapping rows fit many shapes in the height of a few, and an order such as time lets the eye follow a drift down the page. Without a meaningful order the overlaps only hide parts of each curve.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a ridgeline from line-histogram outlines on staggered baselines, until a story needs its own form.
rules.sketch_alt: Five filled curves on evenly spaced baselines, one row a year, whose peak drifts to the right from the top row to the bottom.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how a distribution’s shape drifted across many years or ranked groups.

use_instead.when: Two years or groups only
A few groups and their quartiles

correct.caption: Five filled curves on evenly spaced baselines, one row a year, whose peak drifts to the right from the top row to the bottom.
correct.label: Ridgeline, a sketch

rules.title: Bin very many points into hexagons when a scatter turns to ink.
rule: Use a hexbin, a reference form, when tens of thousands of points would bury each other in a scatter plot: tile the plot with hexagons of equal size and shade each by the count of points in it, on a sequential scale with its key. State the hexagon’s size and the count each step stands for.

text: Past a few thousand points a scatter plot becomes a solid shape whose dense center and sparse edge look alike. Counting the points in equal tiles restores the density, and a key makes each shade a number.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw hexbins with the sequential palette and a stated tile size, until a story needs its own form.
rules.sketch_alt: A field of hexagons shaded from light to dark by how many points fall in each, densest along a rising diagonal, with a four-step key.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks where very many records cluster on two measures, such as income and rent for every census tract.

use_instead.when: A few dozen points, some of them named
A smooth surface for an expert audience

correct.caption: A field of hexagons shaded from light to dark by how many points fall in each, densest along a rising diagonal, with a four-step key.
correct.label: Hexbin, a sketch

rules.title: Draw a contour or density only for experts, with its smoothing stated.
rule: Use contours or a density surface, a reference form, to show where very many points concentrate on two measures: draw lines of equal density, like a map’s height lines, or shade bands between them, and state the smoothing. Draw the few points that matter on top.

text: Contours draw a dense cloud’s shape as lines, so points the story names can sit on top and stay readable. The smoothing changes the shape, so the reader needs to know it.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw density contours in a specialist piece, from a density the analyst states.
rules.sketch_alt: Three nested contour rings around the densest part of a point cloud, the inner ring the strongest, with a few points outside the outer ring.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks where the bulk of very many records lies on two measures, and the exact counts matter less than the shape.

use_instead.when: Counts a reader can check in each area
A few dozen points the reader can name

correct.caption: Three nested contour rings around the densest part of a point cloud, the inner ring the strongest, with a few points outside the outer ring.
correct.label: Contour or density, a sketch

rules.title: Plot two measures as a scatter, and name only the points the story needs.
rule: Draw one dot a place at its two values, with gridlines both ways and each axis named. Name the place the title names in the view’s red point, or in the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for a state; label a few others in regular weight in the light fill where the data single them out past the margin of error (Rule 14.9); and draw the nation as an open ring in the text’s ink. Draw no fitted line: the reader judges the pattern.

A correlation chart takes the Association label where its title says the two measures move together, and the Finding label where the title states documented figures; either way it carries a note that the pattern does not show one causes the other (Rule 13.1).

text: A scatter shows a relationship as a direction a reader can see without a statistic. Names on every dot turn it into a word cloud, so only the places the story needs carry a name, and the table under the chart names every one.

rules.builders: Form scatter-named: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s54; labels.named names the points in ink, labels.labeled points named in the light fill, labels.reference the open ring, labels.sub a named point’s figure under its name.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether two measures move together across places, and where one place sits against the rest.

use_instead.when: A third measure, such as size, matters
The two measures move together over time for one place
The reader compares one measure across places

correct.caption: Do rents run higher where renters earn more, and where does rent take the largest share of renters’ income?

rules.title: Size each point by a third measure only when its size answers the question.
rule: Draw the scatter plot with each circle’s area set by a third measure (Rule 14.4), the largest drawn first and each with a 1 px outline so overlaps read. Give a key of two circle sizes over the plot, name the circles the title names in the view’s red point while that red stays within 5 percent of the drawing at every width (Rule 05.1), or in the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for the four states here, each with the figure its size stands for, and take the label Rule 14.67 sets by what the title says, with its note.

text: Size lets a large place weigh as much on the page as it does in the country, so a small state at an extreme does not read as the whole story. Setting the area by the value keeps a circle that stands for twice as much at twice the size on the page.

rules.builders: Form bubble-scatter: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s55; encode size for the area; labels.size_key gives the key’s sizes and labels.size_key_title its words; labels.sub sets a named circle’s figure under its name.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether two measures move together and where the largest places, by a third measure such as renter households, sit among them.

use_instead.when: The circle sizes add nothing the question asks
Size alone matters, on a map

correct.caption: Where do the states with the most renter households sit on rent and renters’ income?

rules.title: Join a scatter’s points in time order to show two measures moving together.
rule: Draw one dot a period at its two values and join them in time order with a thin path in the subject ink. Name the first and latest periods and the turns the story needs, with leaders where the path is dense. Break the path where a period lacks a value and name the gap (Rule 14.11). Keep the Association label when the title says the two moved together.

text: A connected scatter shows a relationship and its history in one line: loops, reversals and jumps that two separate lines would leave the reader to piece together. Naming a few periods gives the path its dates, and the table gives every one.

rules.builders: Form connected-scatter: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s56; encode time, x and y; labels.named names periods, labels.gap the missing one.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how two measures moved together over years, such as job openings and unemployment through a recession and a recovery.

use_instead.when: Each measure’s own trend matters more than their relationship, drawn as two aligned panels, each on its own scale
Two measures across places at one time

correct.caption: How have unemployment and job openings moved together?

rules.title: Use a correlogram only to scan many variables for experts.
rule: Use a correlogram, a reference form, to show the correlation between every pair of a set of variables as a grid: each cell shaded on a diverging scale from negative to positive, with the coefficient printed in it. Order the variables so related ones sit together, and say which coefficient the cells hold.

text: A grid of coefficients puts dozens of pairs in one view, but a coefficient hides the shape of each relationship. It suits a first scan by experts, before the pairs that matter get charts of their own.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a correlogram with diverging pair B and the coefficient printed in each cell.
rules.sketch_alt: A five-by-five grid of squares, each shaded on a diverging scale by the correlation between two variables, dark at the strongest pairs and pale near zero.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks which of many measures move together before choosing pairs to study.

use_instead.when: One pair of measures
A few variables, each pair worth seeing as points

correct.caption: A five-by-five grid of squares, each shaded on a diverging scale by the correlation between two variables, dark at the strongest pairs and pale near zero.
correct.label: Correlogram, a sketch

rules.title: Use a pair plot to show every pair of a few variables as small scatters.
rule: Use a pair plot, a reference form, for three to five variables: a grid of small scatter plots, one for each pair, with each variable’s histogram on the diagonal. Keep one scale down each column and across each row.

text: Small scatters show each relationship’s shape, which a coefficient cannot, and the shared scales let the eye run along a row. Past five variables the cells grow too small to read.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a pair plot from small scatter-named panels with histogram panels on the diagonal.
rules.sketch_alt: A three-by-three grid: small scatter plots of each pair of three variables off the diagonal, and a small histogram of each variable on it.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how a few measures relate to one another, pair by pair, before choosing which to chart.

use_instead.when: Many variables at once
One pair the story turns on

correct.caption: A three-by-three grid: small scatter plots of each pair of three variables off the diagonal, and a small histogram of each variable on it.
correct.label: Pair plot, a sketch

rules.title: Draw a trajectory to show the pace of change along a path.
rule: Use a trajectory or speed chart, a reference form, to show how fast something moved along a path: dots at equal time steps along a connected path, so wide spacing means fast change and close spacing slow. Mark the start and end and name the steps.

text: Equal time steps turn the spacing of the dots into speed, which a plain path hides. The reader sees where change raced and where it stalled.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a trajectory from connected-scatter with dots at equal time steps.
rules.sketch_alt: A curved path with dots at equal time steps, spaced wide where change ran fast and close together where it slowed, from a start dot to an end dot.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how fast two measures moved along their path, as well as where they went.

use_instead.when: The relationship over time, without the pace
One measure’s rate of change over time

correct.caption: A curved path with dots at equal time steps, spaced wide where change ran fast and close together where it slowed, from a start dot to an end dot.
correct.label: Trajectory or speed chart, a sketch

rules.title: Avoid two value scales on one chart, which can make any two lines cross.
rule: Leave dual-axis line charts out of every Oath & Action piece. Draw two measures as two aligned panels, one above the other, each on its own scale from a stated base and sharing one time axis, or index both to one start date on one scale (Rule 14.4).

text: With two scales the builder chooses where each line sits, so the same data can show the lines crossing, running together or far apart. Readers take the crossing for a finding, though it is only where two scales were placed.

rules.builders: No kit form, by design; for aligned panels draw each measure as its own line-data-gap chart (s31) over the same years, one above the other, each on its own scale from a stated base, or index both with indexed-line (s33).
rules.sketch_alt: The same two invented series drawn twice: on two value scales the lines cross in the middle, and in two aligned panels, each on its own scale from zero, neither line crosses anything, so no false meeting point appears.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how two measures moved over the same years gets a truer answer from two aligned panels.

use_instead.when: Growth compared from one start date
The two measures plotted against each other over time

correct.caption: The same two invented series drawn twice: on two value scales the lines cross in the middle, and in two aligned panels, each on its own scale from zero, neither line crosses anything, so no false meeting point appears.
correct.label: Dual-axis line, a form that misleads

rules.title: Draw a survey figure with its margin of error, and single out only what passes it.
rule: Draw each estimate as a dot on a thin line across its interval, the interval’s level named in the measure line, such as “90 percent margin of error”. Print the margin the publisher gives for the figure drawn, from the same release where it gives one, as the Census Bureau does in its data profile and subject tables, and compute one by its published formula only where it gives none, saying so in the note. With no margin to print or compute, leave the intervals out, set no figure above another, and say in the note that the publisher gives none. Draw the nation as a dashed line in the text’s ink with its own label (Rule 14.6). A dot that differs from the nation by more than the gap’s own margin takes a solid fill; one within it takes an open dot (Rule 14.9). Where a narrow plot leaves the middle row’s interval too short to show past its dot, draw smaller dots, and where even those hide it, drop the lines, print each figure’s margin beside it and say so in a note; the dot stays, filled or open, since it carries the test. List rows by their figures and print each one, but never number them as ranks.

text: A survey figure stands for a range of likely values, and two places whose ranges overlap may stand in either order. Drawing the range and testing each gap keeps the chart from claiming more than the survey knows.

rules.builders: Form range-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s57; encode category, value and margin (or low and high); labels.reference draws the dashed line, labels.test "reference" the open dots, labels.value the right column’s words; encode.margin takes the column the sidecar’s margin_columns names for the value, and a column in check_only_columns serves the data check alone.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how places compare on a survey figure, and how sure each one is.

use_instead.when: A count with no sampling margin
One figure over time with its margin each year
A projection with a range that widens ahead

correct.caption: How do women’s earnings compare with men’s in each state, and how sure is each figure?

rules.title: Draw a band around a line to show each year’s margin of error.
rule: Draw the series as a 2 px line in the subject ink over a band from each year’s low to its high at the publisher’s stated confidence, which the measure line names. Fill the band in the palest gray and draw its two edges as 1 px lines in the context ink, since the fill alone is too pale to see. Where the publisher changed its method, break the line and the band and draw both estimates for that year (Rule 14.11). Label the latest figure with its margin at the line’s end.

text: A band shows at once which year-to-year moves are larger than the survey’s own uncertainty and which sit inside it. Breaking it where the method changed keeps a new questionnaire from reading as a change in people’s lives.

rules.builders: Form line-confidence-band: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s58; encode x, y and margin (or low and high), with break and labels.break_end and labels.break_start for a change of method. The form fills the band in magnitude step 1, the palest of the Stone steps in Rule 14.5, and draws its two edges in the context ink.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a survey figure changed over years and how sure each year’s figure is.

use_instead.when: Places compared at one time
A projection whose range widens ahead
A count with no sampling margin

correct.caption: How has the typical household’s income changed, and how sure is each year’s figure?

rules.title: Show where each outcome would move under each scenario, in words and arrows, with no numbers.
rule: Set scenarios in rows and outcomes in columns, and print the source’s own words for each direction in every cell, with an arrow and a tint read from those words and labeled as Oath & Action’s reading. Print no number, total or odds the source does not give. Say in the grade line that the directions are conditional, with no forecast and no odds. On a phone each scenario becomes a card (Rule 14.12).

text: A direction stated in words is all a scenario claims, so the chart keeps the words and adds only an arrow a reader can check against them. Numbers or odds would claim a precision the scenarios never had.

rules.builders: Form scenario-directions: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s06; encode row, columns and classes, with the arrows and tints read from the classes.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which way each outcome would move if a reform path were followed, and the source states directions with no amounts.

use_instead.when: The source gives numbers for each scenario and their range
Options against criteria, with words and no direction

correct.caption: If a reform path were followed, which way would each outcome move?

rules.title: Draw a projection as a fan whose bands widen with the years ahead.
rule: Draw the median projection as a line in the subject ink with a dot and its value at each period, over two nested bands: the outer from past forecast errors in Stone step 1, and the inner, such as the range of every forecaster’s projection, in Stone step 2. Name the bands in a key, print the outer band’s ends at the last period, and name its probability in the measure line. A period with no date, such as the longer run, sits apart past a thin rule.

text: A single projected line reads as a promise. The widening bands show how much less anyone knows about later years, and drawing them from past errors grounds the range in the record of past forecasts.

rules.builders: Form fan-chart: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s59; encode x, y and the outer and inner bands; labels.apart sets a period apart, labels.key_outer, key_inner and key_median name the key.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where forecasters expect a measure to go and how wide the range of outcomes is.

use_instead.when: Survey margins around figures already measured
Directions under scenarios, with no numbers

correct.caption: Where do Federal Reserve officials expect unemployment to go, and how wide is the range?

rules.title: Show uncertainty as a run of possible outcomes only for experts, with each draw as a still panel.
rule: Use hypothetical outcomes, a reference form, to show uncertainty as several possible results drawn from the estimate’s range, set side by side as small panels or shown one after another. Label every draw as one possible outcome, and pair the form with a band or a range that a still image and a screen reader carry.

text: Seeing several possible results makes uncertainty concrete in a way a shaded band does not. Motion alone fails print, still images and readers who turn animation off, so each draw also stands as a still panel.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw hypothetical outcomes as small panels from small-multiple-bars, each one draw from the stated range.
rules.sketch_alt: Six small panels, each one possible outcome drawn from the same estimate, with a dashed line marking the threshold; the bar lands above it in four panels and below it in two.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how often an outcome would land above or below a line, and a band alone hides how the draws vary together.

use_instead.when: A survey figure and its margin
A projection and its range

correct.caption: Six small panels, each one possible outcome drawn from the same estimate, with a dashed line marking the threshold; the bar lands above it in four panels and below it in two.
correct.label: Hypothetical outcomes, a sketch

rules.title: Set one figure large when a reader should remember it, with the context to judge it.
rule: Print the one figure the reader should carry away in the display face, with the words that say what it counts directly under it, and set beside it the context that makes it mean something: the groups it splits into, a related recorded vote, with everything the bill held, or the figure it compares with. Name every group in words, in neutral inks where parties are concerned (Rule 14.7).

text: Readers remember and repeat a large figure. On its own it invites the reader to supply the comparison, so the context sits in the same view, in the same measure, and the figure keeps its source and its date.

rules.builders: Form big-number: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s01; labels.big_key names the row set large, labels.bars the groups beside it, and labels.votes the recorded votes.
rules.use_when: The reader asks one question with one answer, such as whether Republicans and Democrats agree on a ban on stock trading by members of Congress, and the answer needs a little context to be judged.

use_instead.when: Four to six figures are read together
The figure is a count toward a threshold
The figure sits against a target and ranges
A sentence carries the figure better than a drawing

correct.caption: Do Republicans and Democrats agree on anything about Congress?

rules.title: Use an indicator row for a small set of headline figures read together.
rule: Set four to six figures side by side, each under a hairline with its kind in small words, the figure in the display face in the text’s ink and its caption under it; past six, run on into a second row. Where the captions run long, as the atlas’s do, set each figure beside its caption, one to a row, so a caption keeps to three or four lines. Print each figure exactly as its source stores it and keep its qualification in the notes or the table. An indicator row reports a set, so it takes no fill and no red.

text: Figures in a row are read one by one, each with its own words, so a reader can take any one away without the others. Printing each as stored keeps the row from rounding or restating a figure its source never gave.

rules.builders: Form indicator-row: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s60; encode.figure, encode.caption and encode.kind name the columns, labels.kinds the printed kind words and labels.columns the most in a row, and labels.beside sets each figure beside its caption, one to a row, wherever the caption’s column holds 240 px.
rules.use_when: The reader asks for the headline numbers on a subject, such as the atlas’s eight figures, and each figure stands on its own.

use_instead.when: One figure is the point
The figures share a measure and should be compared
The figures change over time and the trend matters

correct.caption: What are the atlas’s headline figures?

rules.title: Use a progress bar for a count toward a threshold.
rule: Draw one bar that runs to the whole, such as the 100 senators, with the count from zero in the red point while its red stays within 5 percent of the drawing at every width (Rule 05.1), or in the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for a vote, and the rest in the track gray. Where the count is a vote, draw the other side as a segment of its own in outline in the same ink (Rule 01.2), so each side of the vote has a mark. Mark the threshold with a tick in the text’s ink and its words over it, bracket the gap between the count and the threshold under the bar with its words, and name what fills the count and the rest under the bar, each party by name where the count is a vote (Rule 14.7).

text: A bar that runs to the whole shows the count, the threshold and the distance between them as lengths on one scale. The bracket and its words say the shortfall outright, so no reader has to subtract.
The specimen draws the Senate vote that Rule 14.85’s specimen sets beside a survey, here as a count toward the 60 votes that end debate.

rules.builders: Form progress-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s61; encode.value and encode.against name each group’s count and rest, and labels.of, labels.needed and their words set the whole and the threshold; labels.ink “party” and labels.rest “outline” draw a vote’s two sides in the party-mark ink, one solid and one in outline.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how close a count came to the number it needed, such as the votes to end debate in the Senate.

use_instead.when: The measure sits against a target and ranges
Several counts are compared with one threshold
One figure with its context answers it

correct.caption: How close did the Senate come to the 60 votes it needs to end debate on taking up H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act?

rules.title: Use a step tracker to show where one bill stands in its six steps.
rule: Draw the bill’s six steps as chapter 11 sets them (Rules 11.1 to 11.3): numbered circles, filled for a step done, a heavy ring on the step the bill is at now, a fine ring on a step ahead, and a slash through the number of a step that never happened. Give each step its name, its state in words with its date, and a short note; run the steps across where each one’s sixth of the row holds its date, and down the page where it does not (Rule 11.6). End with the words that say where the bill stands.

text: A reader who follows bills learns one set of six marks and reads every tracker the same way, across a page or down it. A slashed step keeps the count at six, so a skipped hearing shows as a step that never happened.

rules.builders: Form step-tracker: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s62; labels.steps gives each step’s name, the action codes that mark it done and its note, and labels.became the end words.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where one bill is in its path to law, or how it got there, such as a bill that skipped its committee.

use_instead.when: Many bills are followed at once
The dates themselves are the point
The record’s status is a word, with no steps to follow

correct.caption: Where is a bill in its stages, from introduction to law?

rules.title: Use status chips to give each record’s status in a word.
rule: Give each record its status in a chip as chapter 18 draws one: the word in the label style on a hairline edge in the text’s ink, one style for every status, so the word carries the status. Lead each record with its typed ID in its own chip (Rule 13.9) and its title as the record stores it, in regular weight, then the words that give the status its case or finding and its date, then the date the record was checked.

text: A word in a chip is read faster than a sentence and holds its meaning in gray print and for a reader who sees no color. One style for every status keeps color from ranking them, and the words under each chip let a reader check the status against its source.

rules.builders: Form status-chips: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s63; labels.status gives each record’s chip word and its words, labels.id_type the type word in each ID chip.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where a set of disputes or measures stands now, such as six disputes over checks on power.

use_instead.when: A record moves through set steps
The reader looks up one record among many
Each record carries several measures to compare

correct.caption: Where do six disputes over checks on power stand?

rules.title: Use a bullet graph to set one measure against its target and the ranges behind it.
rule: Draw the ranges as gray bands from zero, a shade apart, the measure as a narrow bar in the subject ink from zero, and the target as a tick in the text’s ink across the bands. A range can be a past target, such as an earlier limit, and its words say so. Name every band edge and the target with its figure once over the rows, and print the measure and its distance to the target beside each bar.

text: A bar from zero keeps the measure honest at any distance from its target, and the bands behind it give the scale meaning without a dial or a color code. The printed distance says the answer in the reader’s units.

rules.builders: Form bullet-graph: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s64; encode.target names the target column, labels.bands the bands, each with its magnitude step (1 to 4, the Stone steps of Rule 14.5) and words, and labels.per divides the printed figures.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how close one measure is to a target or a limit, such as federal debt against the limit set in law, and the ranges give it meaning.

use_instead.when: The measure is a count toward a threshold with nothing behind it
Several measures are compared with one benchmark each
The measure’s path over time is the point

correct.caption: How close is federal debt to the limit set in law?

rules.title: Avoid gauges, whose angle is harder to read than a bar’s length.
rule: Leave dials, speedometers and other gauges out of every Oath & Action piece. Draw the same value as a progress bar toward its threshold, or as a bullet graph where a target and ranges matter, so it is read as a length from zero.

text: A gauge asks the reader to judge an angle on a curved scale, which they do less exactly than a length on a straight one. Its needle, face and color zones take room and ink that a bar spends on the value.

rules.builders: No form: the kit draws no gauge. The sketch, work/build/guide/specimens/s-14-91-sketch.html, draws a gauge beside a progress bar of the same values; build the better choice with progress-bar or bullet-graph.
rules.sketch_alt: A gauge sets an illustrative 70 of 100 as a needle’s angle on a dial, and a progress bar of the same values shows it as a length a reader can measure against the mark at 80. The bar needs no dial to read.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how close a measure is to a mark gets a truer answer from a progress bar or a bullet graph.

use_instead.when: The value is a count toward a threshold
The value sits against a target and ranges

correct.caption: A gauge sets an illustrative 70 of 100 as a needle’s angle on a dial, and a progress bar of the same values shows it as a length a reader can measure against the mark at 80.
correct.label: Gauge, a form that misleads

rules.title: Avoid thermometers, which spend ink on a tube and a bulb that carry no value.
rule: Leave thermometers, the tubes with a bulb used for fundraising goals, out of every Oath & Action piece. Draw the same count as a progress bar toward its goal, with the goal marked and the amount still to go printed.

text: A thermometer is a bar with a bulb at its foot, so the bulb and the tube’s rounded ends add ink with no value. A plain bar from zero shows the same share and leaves room to print the goal and the gap.

rules.builders: No form: the kit draws no thermometer. The sketch, work/build/guide/specimens/s-14-92-sketch.html, draws a thermometer beside a progress bar of the same values; build the better choice with progress-bar.
rules.sketch_alt: A thermometer fills an illustrative 70 percent of a goal inside a tube with a bulb, and a progress bar of the same values shows the share with the goal marked and less ink. The bulb holds no value.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how close a total is to its goal gets the same answer from a progress bar with less ink.

use_instead.when: The value is a count toward a goal
The value sits against a target and ranges

correct.caption: A thermometer fills an illustrative 70 percent of a goal inside a tube with a bulb, and a progress bar of the same values shows the share with the goal marked and less ink.
correct.label: Thermometer, a form that misleads

rules.title: Use a funnel when people pass through stages and some leave at each.
rule: Draw each stage as a bar from one left edge, each inside the one before, so every stage reads against the first by length, and print each stage’s count and its share of the first. Beside each bar, draw what the stage lost as a segment from its end to the end of the stage before, and name it under the segment. The loss the title names takes the text’s ink, and stages and other losses are gray (Rule 14.6). Set a group still waiting, decided neither way, apart below the stages, and keep the parts of a stage in the table.

text: A funnel puts the start and every stage on one scale, so a reader sees how many remain and where the largest loss came. Bars from one edge compare more exactly than the centered funnel shape, which makes the eye judge widths from the middle.

rules.builders: Form funnel: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s65; encode category, value, key and role (labels.stage marks a stage); labels.losses maps each stage to the loss before it, labels.apart sets a group aside below the stages, labels.named takes the loss the title names into the subject ink; stages take the light fill with the context edge.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how many people made it through each step of a process, and where the rest left.

use_instead.when: Steps of a process with the time each may take
Parts of one whole with no order
One group followed over time until an event

correct.caption: Of the people whose Medicaid or CHIP coverage came up for renewal, how many had a decision, how many were not cut off for paperwork, and how many kept coverage?

rules.title: Use a cohort chart to follow groups that started at different times.
rule: Use a cohort chart, a reference form, to track groups that began at different times, such as the people who enrolled in a program each year, on one clock that starts when each group began. Draw one line for each group, with the years since its start along the bottom and the share still enrolled up the side, from 100 percent at the start, and name each line at its end by its start year. Keep to four groups, or set the one the title names in the text’s ink and the rest in gray (Rule 14.8).

text: Lining groups up by the time since they started sets each against the others at the same stage. The clock that starts at each group’s own start needs explaining, so the form suits reports and specialists more than a quick read.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a cohort chart with one line a group in the subject ink or the context ink, labeled at its end, on a shared start-time axis.
rules.sketch_alt: Four lines, one for each year’s starting group, falling from 100 percent as the years since the start pass, with the latest group in the text’s ink.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks whether people who started later stay longer or leave sooner than those who started earlier.

use_instead.when: One group and the time until an event
One measure across calendar years

correct.caption: Four lines, one for each year’s starting group, falling from 100 percent as the years since the start pass, with the latest group in the text’s ink.
correct.label: Cohort chart, a sketch

rules.title: Use a survival curve to show how long until an event happens.
rule: Use a survival curve, a reference form, to show the share of a group that has not yet reached an event, such as a case still open or a person still enrolled, at each point after its start. Draw a step line from 100 percent that drops at each event, mark each person who left before the event with a small tick, and print the time at which half the group had reached it. Name the group, the start and the event in the measure line.

text: A step line keeps each drop at the moment it happened, so the curve shows when the event comes fastest. People whose outcome is not yet known stay in the count until they leave, which a plain share of those who reached the event would miss.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a survival curve as a step line in the subject ink, with ticks for people who left before the event.
rules.sketch_alt: A step line falling from 100 percent as time passes, with small ticks where people left before the event and a thin line where half the group had reached it.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how long cases or people last before something happens to them.

use_instead.when: Several groups by their start date
Counts of people at fixed stages

correct.caption: A step line falling from 100 percent as time passes, with small ticks where people left before the event and a thin line where half the group had reached it.
correct.label: Survival curve, a sketch

rules.title: Use a process diagram to show the steps an institution takes to decide, and where others can step in.
rule: Number the steps of the main path, as the law lays them out, and run them down one heavy line in order, each in a box with an edge in the text’s ink that names the step, who acts and the time the law sets. Set each branch a case may take beside the step it leaves or enters, in a box with a gray edge and a short line that says when it applies, joined by a gray arrow (Rule 14.6); arrows on the main line point the way a case moves. Print the date of the law the diagram draws, and give the table every step and branch in the order a reader meets them, each with where it leads. On a phone the steps run in one column, a step’s way in above it and its branches below it, set in from the line.

text: One line through the steps every case takes lets a reader learn the main path first, and the branches beside it show where the path can turn without hiding it. Numbers keep the order when the diagram is read aloud or as a table.

rules.builders: Form process-diagram: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s66; encode.path marks the main steps with labels.main, labels.branches gives each branch the step it leaves or enters (at), its way (dir, out or in) and its line of words, and the table sorts by encode.key’s values in reading order.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how an institution makes or changes something, such as how an agency writes a rule, and where Congress, a court or the public can step in.

use_instead.when: One bill or rule’s place in its steps is the question
The reader picks a path by answering questions about their own place
The question is how long each step can take for one person

correct.caption: How does a federal agency make or change a rule, and where can Congress or a court step in?

rules.title: Use a decision tree when the answer turns on facts about the reader’s own place.
rule: Put the question in a box with an edge in the text’s ink and each answer under it in a shaded box, joined by arrows of one weight, every answer drawn alike (Rule 14.6). Open each answer with its word and how many places it holds, then what it means, then the places by name where the list is short; a further question sits in its own box under the answer that leads to it. Print the date the facts were checked. On a phone the answers run down the page, set in from a line at the left, and the table lists every place in the tree’s order with the answer it takes.

text: A reader answers one question at a time and finds their own case at the end, with the count of places that share it. Drawing every answer alike keeps the tree from steering a reader toward any one of them.

rules.builders: Form decision-tree: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s67; labels.tree gives the question and its answers, each with a where over the rows that it counts, its count words with {n}, its meaning, list to name the places and then for a further question.
rules.use_when: The reader asks a yes-or-no question whose answer depends on their state or city, such as whether a city may switch its own elections to ranked-choice voting.

use_instead.when: Every state’s answer at once is the point
Everyone follows the same steps
A reader looks up one place in a long list

correct.caption: Can my city switch its own elections to ranked-choice voting?

rules.title: Use a who-decides diagram to show who can change a rule and who only applies it.
rule: Place each body by what it can do: those who can change the rules in a band above those who apply them, in columns from federal to regional, state, local and private hands, every body in one box style with its name in bold. Draw a line of authority, one body setting or approving another’s rules, as a gray arrow from the body that decides to the one it governs, with no plus or minus sign and no loop, as chapter 15 keeps authority apart from cause (Rule 15.5). On a phone the bands run down the page, each body under its level’s name, with the lines of authority in a lane at the left.

text: Position answers the reader’s first question before they read a single line, since the bodies in the upper band can change the rules. A line of authority says who decides and leaves the choice open, as the atlas records it, so it carries no sign.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s definition of an authority connection; design judgment

rules.builders: Form who-decides: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s68; encode.changes sets the band, encode.level the column (labels.levels and labels.level_words), labels.authority the lines from one body’s key to another’s and labels.order the order bodies stack in a column.
rules.use_when: The reader asks who sets something they pay or live under, such as an electric bill, and which of those bodies could change the rules behind it.

use_instead.when: One body’s own structure is the question
The steps of one decision matter more than the bodies
Many bodies trade money or ties, and the links are the point

correct.caption: Who sets my electric bill, and who can change the rules behind it?

rules.title: Use an org chart to show who sits under whom inside one body.
rule: Put the body’s box at the top and run a line down the left to each group of its units, headed with the group’s count. Draw each unit as a card: a named box with the count of units under it and, below it, set in, a box for each of those units, joined by gray elbow lines. Every box takes an edge in the text’s ink. Fill as many columns as the width holds, each card in the shortest column, so the order reads from the top down, and keep any split by party to the table. On a phone the cards run in one column.

text: A reader looking for one committee scans the cards, then reads down to its subcommittees, and the counts tell how the work divides before any name is read. One ink keeps every unit equal, since the question is about the body as a whole.

rules.builders: Form org-chart: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s69; encode.unit and encode.unit_key name each unit, encode.group its group (labels.groups), encode.sub its sub-units; labels.drop sets prefixes a unit’s name leaves off, labels.count the count words.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how one body divides its work, such as the House’s committees and their subcommittees.

use_instead.when: Each part carries a count that sums up the tree
Who can change a rule across several bodies is the question
The parts’ sizes matter more than who sits under whom

correct.caption: How is the House divided into committees and subcommittees?

rules.title: Use a hierarchy tree for parts nested inside parts, with a count at every level.
rule: Put the top part’s box first and run a line down the left to each group of its children, headed with the group’s count. Draw each child as a card that prints its own count and the sum of the counts under it, so the levels add up, and list its parts under it, set in and joined by gray elbow lines, grouped the way a reader looks for them, such as by state. Shade a part of another kind and say what it is in words, and set apart a child that serves the whole tree, named. On a phone the cards run in one column.

text: A reader finds their own part first, then follows the line up to the level that hears its appeal. A count at every level lets the tree be checked by addition, and the shaded parts show at a glance which courts stand on a different footing.

rules.builders: Form hierarchy-tree: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s70; encode.parent links each part to its parent, encode.count gives its count and encode.place groups its parts; labels.card_sub prints {n} and {d}, labels.apart sets children apart, labels.apart_level shades parts of another kind.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where something sits in a nested system and where it leads next, such as which federal court hears a case from their state and where an appeal goes.

use_instead.when: The parts’ sizes are the point
One body’s units sit under it with no count to add up
A reader looks up one part in a long list

correct.caption: Which federal court hears a case from my state, and where does an appeal go?

rules.title: Use a comparison grid to weigh a few options against the same questions in words.
rule: Give each option a row, named in bold, and each question a column, every cell in words in the text’s ink with a thin gray rule between rows. Keep the options in the order their source gives them, and draw a count, where one helps, as a single series of bars with its value printed. Under a cell that rests on a text, print the text and the date it was read. On a phone each option runs as a block: its name and count, then each column’s name over its words.

text: A reader reads across a row to learn one option and down a column to compare them on one question, and words keep the requirements exact where a symbol would round them off. The source under each cell lets a reader check a threshold against its text.

rules.builders: Form comparison-grid: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s71; encode.name names each row and encode.count draws the bar; labels.columns gives each column’s field, label and share of the width, and under_words a line under its cells.
rules.use_when: The reader weighs a handful of options against the same questions, such as what each route to change a law takes and how it can be undone.

use_instead.when: Many rows carry one value each, read by step
Two or three options suit cards side by side
A handful of numbers answers the question

correct.caption: Which of the eleven routes can carry a reform, and what does each one take?

rules.title: Use a roll-call grid to show how every member voted, with each party named in words.
rule: Draw one square for each member, in one neutral ink for every party (Rule 14.7): solid for yes, an outline for no, shaded for a member who did not vote and a faint outline for a vacant seat. Head each chamber with its vote, its date and the question and result in the record’s words. Give each party a row of its own, named in words with its count and how it voted, Democrats first, independents as the record lists them, folded into no party, and Republicans last, with vacant seats between, as the chart for Rule 14.53 orders the sides (Rule 14.7).

text: A square for each member lets a reader count the members who crossed party lines without a key to colors, and solid against outline in one ink tells yes from no in gray print and for a reader who sees no color. Naming each party in words keeps the sides clear with no red and blue.

rules.builders: Form roll-call-grid: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s72; labels.chambers, labels.parties and labels.votes set the order, labels.seats each chamber’s seats so the vacant count follows, labels.head and labels.ask the panel’s words from the record.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how each member of a chamber voted on one bill, and how many from each party crossed over.

use_instead.when: Only the totals matter, against the votes a rule needs
The chamber’s seats are the question, with no vote
How members voted across many bills

correct.caption: How did each senator and representative vote on the November 2025 bill that ended the shutdown?

rules.title: Keep a mind map for sorting ideas, and publish a diagram that shows how the parts connect.
rule: Use a mind map, a reference form, while a story is being planned: one topic in the middle, its parts on lines around it, and their own parts beyond them. Before it reaches a reader, turn it into the form that shows how the parts relate, a process diagram for steps in order, a hierarchy tree for parts with counts or a table for a list.

text: Lines around a center say only that two ideas belong together. A reader also needs to know how they relate, whether one comes before another, sits under it or causes it, and the forms built for each relation draw it.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a mind map only as a sketch for planning; build process-diagram or hierarchy-tree for a reader.
rules.sketch_alt: A mind map of an illustrative city budget, one topic in the middle with four parts on lines around it and a further idea beside each. The lines say each part belongs to the budget, and nothing about order or size.
rules.use_when: Writers and editors sort the parts of a subject before they know how the parts connect, such as the topics a guide to a city budget might cover.

use_instead.when: The parts follow one another in order
The parts nest inside one another with counts
The parts are a list a reader scans

correct.caption: A mind map of an illustrative city budget, one topic in the middle with four parts on lines around it and a further idea beside each.
correct.label: Mind map, a sketch

rules.title: Use a network diagram to show who sent what to whom.
rule: Draw each sender and each receiver as a bar as tall as its amount, with its name and amount beside it, and join them with links whose width is the amount, in one linear unit for the whole drawing, with a key of widths (Rule 14.4). Stack the links that leave a bar in the order of the bars they reach, so none cross. Fold many small receivers of one kind into one bar with their count, and list each in the table. Draw two sides alike, side by side and in one ink, and name each side in words; money spent to elect a candidate takes one neutral ink for every party, with no red or blue (Rules 14.6 and 14.7).

text: Bars and links on one scale let a reader compare every sender and receiver of both sides at a glance, and names set beside the bars keep each end readable on a phone. Folding many small receivers keeps the drawing calm, and the table keeps every one.

rules.builders: Form network-diagram: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s73; encode source, target, value, target_key and kind; labels.nodes folds rows into nodes, labels.unit sets the measure one pixel of width carries, labels.key_steps the key, labels.ink the party-mark ink; draws its bars as tall as their dollars in the links’ unit, through K.parts.flows, flow_band and width_key.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where money or influence went from a few senders, and which links carried the most.

use_instead.when: Money into one account and out of it
Many parts with many links among them
Links among items in a set order

correct.caption: Where did each 2024 presidential nominee’s joint fundraising committee send what it raised?

rules.title: Use an adjacency matrix when many parts link to many others.
rule: Draw one row for each part a link starts from and one column for each part it reaches, in the same order, and shade each cell by its count on a sequential scale, with the count printed in it; leave an empty cell as the page inside a thin grid line. Group the parts with a gap between groups, number the columns and name the rows; on a phone, number the rows too and list the names under the grid. Give a class of links that differs in kind, such as lines of authority with no sign, an outline and a key entry of its own, apart from the scale’s steps.

text: A grid never tangles, however many links it holds, and its rows and columns let a reader find any pair. It gives up the paths a network shows, so it suits counts between groups more than one route.

rules.builders: Form adjacency-matrix: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s74; encode from, to, value and special (the count in the class with no sign); labels.order sets the parts, labels.groups the gaps, labels.steps the scale with its fills (seq-1 takes the context edge), labels.special_label the outlined class.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which parts of a system connect to which, and the links are too many for lines to stay readable.

use_instead.when: A few senders and the amounts they sent
Links among items in a set order
Values across two categories, with no links

correct.caption: Which parts of the atlas connect to which?

rules.title: Use an arc diagram for links among items in a set order.
rule: Set the items on one line in an order that means something, such as the date each was introduced, and join each linked pair with an arc above the line whose width is the pair’s count, in one linear unit with a key of widths (Rule 14.4). Draw the widest arcs first so narrow ones stay in view, name each item under the line, and set the pair the title names in the text’s ink with every other arc gray (Rule 14.6). On a phone, run the line down the left and bow the arcs to the right. Print every pair and its count in the table.

text: Keeping the items in their own order lets a reader see whether linked items sit close together or far apart. Arcs cross one another, so the form holds a few dozen links before the table must carry the detail.

rules.builders: Form arc-diagram: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s75; encode from, to and value; labels.order sets the line, labels.unit the px of width per unit, labels.named the pair in the subject ink, labels.split breaks “H.R. 950” over two lines; draws through K.parts.link with shape arc and K.parts.width_key.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which items in a list share something, such as bills that drew the same backers, and the list has an order worth keeping.

use_instead.when: Many parts with many links among them
Amounts sent from a few senders

correct.caption: Which House bills to rein in drug middlemen drew the same backers?

rules.title: Use a chord diagram only for flows among a few groups, for specialists.
rule: Use a chord diagram, a reference form, to show flows both ways among a few groups: each group an arc on a circle, sized by its total, and each flow a ribbon between two arcs, as wide at each end as the amount it carries from that side. Keep to five groups or fewer, name each arc outside the circle, and draw the ribbons gray, with the one the title names in the text’s ink (Rule 14.6).

text: A circle shows every pair and both directions in one view, but ribbons that bend around it are hard to compare by width. A matrix or a Sankey gives the same amounts more exactly to a general reader.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a chord diagram with ribbons in the context ink and the named ribbon in the subject ink.
rules.sketch_alt: Four arcs around a circle, one for each group, joined by gray ribbons as wide as the flows between them, with one ribbon in the text’s ink.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how much flows each way among a few groups, such as people moving among four regions.

use_instead.when: Flows from sources to uses in one direction
Counts between many groups

correct.caption: Four arcs around a circle, one for each group, joined by gray ribbons as wide as the flows between them, with one ribbon in the text’s ink.
correct.label: Chord diagram, a sketch

rules.title: Use a multi-network only where the kinds of links are the story.
rule: Use a multi-network, a reference form, to draw more than one kind of link among the same nodes, such as shared money and shared staff among a set of groups. Give each kind of link its own ink in the chart order, solid, and name it in a key and on one of its lines; never a dash or dot, which Rule 13.4 keeps for a connection’s grade. Keep to three kinds; past that, draw one panel for each kind with every node in the same place.

text: Each kind in its own ink and named on its line holds in grayscale, since the names carry the kinds where the inks merge. More than three kinds tangle, and panels with fixed places keep each kind readable.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a multi-network with K.parts.node and K.parts.link, one categorical ink a kind of link (cat-1, then cat-2, then cat-3), solid, each kind named on one of its lines with K.parts.clear_label and in a key.
rules.sketch_alt: Five nodes joined by solid lines in two inks, one for each kind of tie, each kind named in a key and on one of its lines.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how two or three kinds of ties overlap among the same people or groups.

use_instead.when: One kind of link with an amount
Links counted between groups

correct.caption: Five nodes joined by solid lines in two inks, one for each kind of tie, each kind named in a key and on one of its lines.
correct.label: Multi-network, a sketch

rules.title: Draw a tie that runs both ways as one line with no arrowhead.
rule: Use symmetrical links, a reference form, where a tie means the same from either end, such as two agencies that share board members: draw each tie as one plain line with no arrowhead, as thick as its count, such as shared members, with a key of widths (Rule 14.4). Where a tie runs one way, give it an arrowhead (Rule 14.104), and where the two ways carry different amounts, draw two arcs, each with its own arrowhead and width.

text: An arrowhead claims a direction, and on a shared tie it would invent one. One plain line says the tie is shared.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw each tie with K.parts.link and no arrow, its width the tie’s count, with K.parts.width_key.
rules.sketch_alt: Four nodes joined by plain lines with no arrowheads, each line as thick as the tie it draws.
rules.use_when: The reader asks who is tied to whom, and each tie means the same from either end.

use_instead.when: Ties that run one way, with amounts
Flows both ways among a few groups

correct.caption: Four nodes joined by plain lines with no arrowheads, each line as thick as the tie it draws.
correct.label: Symmetrical links, a sketch

rules.title: Use a Sankey to show money into one account and out of it.
rule: Draw each source as a band from the left into one node and each use as a band from the node to the right, every band as wide as its amount in one linear unit, with a key band (Rule 14.4), so the bands sum at the node. Put the money on hand at the start first on the left and at the end last on the right, so the node balances, and give any remainder the record leaves in a note.
