Group loans and their repayments apart by a gap under their own names, so a reader can tell a loan from a gift, and say in a note that the chart traces no dollar received to a dollar spent. The flow the title names takes the text’s ink; the rest are gray with a thin edge (Rule 14.6).

text: Bands on one scale show the largest sources and uses at a glance and keep the account’s balance in view. Small lines shrink to a hairline at that scale, so each band prints its amount and the table keeps every cent.

rules.builders: Form sankey: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s76; encode side, key, category and value; labels.groups sets bands apart under a name, labels.track the cash on hand, labels.named the flow in the subject ink, labels.open lets the node keep the record’s remainder; draws through K.parts.flows, flow_band and width_key.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where an account’s money came from and where it went, in one period.

use_instead.when: Money sent from a few senders to receivers
Lines that add and subtract to a total
Parts of one total in one year

correct.caption: Where did the money for 2024 House campaigns come from, and where did it go?

rules.title: Use an alluvial chart only where the same people are counted at each time.
rule: Use an alluvial chart, a reference form, to show how one group’s choices changed between two or three times, such as the plans the same people chose in two years of a panel survey: each time a column of stacked blocks, and bands between the columns as wide as the people who moved from one block to another. Draw it only from data that follow the same people; a survey that asks different people each time cannot show who moved.

text: Bands between columns show who stayed and who switched, which two separate totals cannot. The bands mean something only when each person is the same at both times.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw an alluvial chart with K.parts.flow_band between two stacked columns, bands in the context ink and the named band in the subject ink.
rules.sketch_alt: Two columns of three stacked blocks, joined by gray bands as wide as the people who stayed or moved between them, with one band in the text’s ink.
rules.use_when: A specialist asks how the same people moved between choices from one time to the next.

use_instead.when: Totals at two times, from different people
Money into one account and out of it

correct.caption: Two columns of three stacked blocks, joined by gray bands as wide as the people who stayed or moved between them, with one band in the text’s ink.
correct.label: Alluvial, a sketch

rules.title: Use a journey map to show a person’s path through a public service, step by step.
rule: Draw each step as a box with its name, who acts and the time the rule allows, joined in order by arrows, and draw a branch some people take from the step it leaves. Print each time as the rule’s limit, say in the measure line that the chart measures no wait, and print the date of the rule. The main path is in the text’s ink and a branch is gray (Rule 14.6). At a desk the path reads across; on a phone it reads down, with the branch after the last step. The table lists the steps in reading order, each with the step that follows it.

text: A journey map follows the person who applies, so a reader finds their own place in the process and the longest they may wait. Calling each time a limit keeps a reader from taking it as a promise.

rules.builders: Form journey-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s77; encode step, path, key, who and limit; labels.limits gives each step’s time in words, labels.branch_label names who takes the branch, labels.across_from sets the width where the path turns down; draws through K.parts.node and K.parts.link.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what happens after they apply, sign up or file, and how long each step can take.

use_instead.when: How a rule or a law is made, with its branches
Counts of people who made it through each step
Steps a reader takes, with no times

correct.caption: What happens after someone applies for SNAP food benefits, and how long can each step take?

rules.title: Use a flow map only when the routes between places answer the question.
rule: Use a flow map, a reference form, to show how many people, goods or dollars moved between places: a line from each origin to each destination over a plain map, as wide as the amount it carries on one scale, with an arrowhead where it arrives and a key of two widths. Draw the lines under the place names, keep the few largest flows and say how many the map leaves out, and give every flow’s amount in the table.

text: A line between two places gives a route a reader can follow, and its width shows how much moved along it. Past a few dozen lines the routes cross into a tangle, so the form suits a few large flows or a single origin.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw each flow as a curve in the subject ink under the place dots and names, its stroke width set by one scale (amount per pixel) with a key of two widths, and an arrowhead at the destination.
rules.sketch_alt: Curved lines run from one place to four others over a plain map, each as wide as the invented number of people who moved along it, with a key of two widths.
rules.use_when: A reader asks where people or money went from a few places, and the routes matter as much as the amounts.

use_instead.when: The amounts matter and the places do not
Moves among many places, in both directions
Each place’s total moving in or out, with no routes

correct.caption: Curved lines run from one place to four others over a plain map, each as wide as the invented number of people who moved along it, with a key of two widths.
correct.label: Flow map, a sketch

rules.title: Use a tile-grid map to show each state’s status, every state the same size.
rule: Draw each state and the District of Columbia as one square of the same size, on a grid that keeps each state beside its neighbors, with Alaska and Hawaii at its corners, and print each state’s two-letter code in its square. Tell the categories apart by fill and outline as well as shade, so the key still reads in gray print: solid squares for the status the title names, open squares for a partial case and gray squares for none, each named in the key. Print one more fact under the code, such as the year a law took effect, wherever the square holds it. Where the squares grow too small for their codes, leave the codes out and say under the map that the table names every state.

text: On a map of real shapes, large, thinly settled states take most of the page, so a status held mostly by small eastern states looks rare. Equal squares give every state the same weight, and the code in each square names the place in words.

rules.builders: Form tile-map-categorical: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s07, or copy specs/s07.json and point it at a new dataset; encode code, category and sub (the line under the code); labels.categories sets each category’s style (solid, open or light) and words, and labels.key_at the key’s place in the grid’s empty upper middle.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which states have a law or status, and each state counts once, whatever its size or population.

use_instead.when: A rate by state, on the shapes readers know
How far each state moved between two dates
The same status at several dates, to show how it spread
The reader looks up one state’s law and its details

correct.caption: Which states prohibit ranked-choice voting?

rules.title: Use a tile map of arrows to show where a measure moved, every state on one scale.
rule: Give each state one square holding an arrow that points the way the measure moved, its length set by the shift on one scale across the map, with the state’s code and the shift printed above the arrow. Name the direction in words in the key, as “toward the Republican nominee”, so no color stands for a party (Rule 14.7). Set the national figure beside the key with its own label and arrow (Rule 14.6), and frame each state whose leader changed.

On a phone, where an arrow would be too short to read, each square takes a gray step by the size of its shift, and two lists under the map name the largest and smallest shifts with their figures (Rule 14.12).

text: A reader compares lengths more surely than shades, so arrows on one scale show at a glance where a shift ran large. The arrows and the words in the key carry the direction, so no party needs a color, and equal squares keep a small state’s move as visible as a large one’s.

rules.builders: Form tile-map-shift-arrows: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s12; encode code, shift, from and to; labels.frame "sign" frames a state whose from and to differ in sign, labels.key_steps sets the sample arrows, labels.steps and steps_labels the phone’s gray steps, labels.nation_label the national figure beside the key, and labels.lists the two lists.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where a measure moved between two dates and how far, state by state, such as a presidential margin from one election to the next.

use_instead.when: The reader asks which places moved most, more than where they sit
The reader looks up how each state voted in each year
Each state has a status with no direction

correct.caption: Where did the presidential margin move between 2020 and 2024?

rules.title: Use a bubble map when the size of each place matters as much as its rate.
rule: Set a circle at each state’s center over the land, its area in proportion to a count such as citizens 18 and over (Rule 14.4), and shade it by a rate in the sequential steps, with a key for each. Move circles apart only where they would overlap, and print each state’s code inside its circle, or beside it with a leader where the circle is too small to hold it (Rule 14.3). Mark the national rate on the step key with its label (Rule 14.6). Ring only the circles the title names, and single out a survey rate only where its gap passes the margin of error (Rule 14.9).

text: On a map of shaded states, land sets how much of the page each state takes, so a large state with few people outweighs a small, crowded one. A circle sized by people gives each state its weight on the page, and its shade adds the rate without a second map.

rules.builders: Form bubble-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s16; encode code, size (the circle’s area) and shade; labels.bins sets the shade’s four breaks, labels.size_steps and size_step_words the size key, labels.ring the circles ringed, labels.nation and nation_label the national rate on the step key, and labels.offsets a code’s place where the search finds none.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where a rate ran high or low and where most of the people are, such as which of the largest states reported low turnout.

use_instead.when: A rate alone, where each state’s size adds nothing
Where a count sits inside the states, county by county
Two measures compared as a pattern, with size as a third

correct.caption: Where did more citizens report voting in 2024?

rules.title: Use a choropleth to show a rate on the shapes of the states, in a few classes a margin of error cannot blur.
rule: Shade each state by its class in the sequential steps, four classes at most, the lightest with a 1 px edge, and draw the borders as thin lines of the page color. Set each class at least as wide as the widest margin of error drawn, and say in a note how many states sit close enough to a class line to fall in the next one (Rule 14.9). Print each state’s code on its shape in its step’s label ink, or beside it with a short leader; draw the District of Columbia as a small square beside Maryland; set Alaska and Hawaii apart in thin frames, and put the national figure above the map with its name (Rule 14.6).

text: A reader finds a state by its shape faster than by a list, and a few classes turn the rates into a pattern at a glance. Classes wider than the survey’s margins keep a state’s shade from claiming more than the survey can tell.

rules.builders: Form choropleth: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s78; encode code, value and margin; labels.bins sets where each class starts, labels.class_labels its words, labels.nation and nation_label the national figure, labels.dc the District of Columbia’s square; the boundary file is the spec’s second dataset.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where a rate runs high or low across the states, and the shape of the country helps them find their own.

use_instead.when: Each state counts once, whatever its size
Size matters as much as the rate
The rate county by county
The reader looks up one state’s exact figure

correct.caption: Where do more households have a broadband internet subscription?

rules.title: Use a locator map to show where a story takes place, with one red point on the place.
rule: Mark the place in the view’s one red point with its keyline and name it (Rule 14.6), with a second, better-known place nearby in the text’s ink for scale. Shade the place’s county lightly with an edge, draw the rest of the state in the track ink and its neighbors as thin gray lines, add a scale bar, and set a small inset of the country with the state shaded and the view outlined on it.

text: A reader who has never been to a place needs a nearby name they know and a sense of distance. The inset answers “which part of the country”, and the main view answers “where in the state”.

rules.builders: Form locator-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s79; encode name, lon and lat; labels.point names the red point’s row, labels.county the county’s geoid, labels.layer a fitted county layer (counties-ca), and labels.neighbors the neighboring states’ names.
rules.use_when: The reader needs to know where a place in the story is, such as the town in a photograph.

use_instead.when: A rate across many places
Movement between places

correct.caption: Where is Lake Isabella, the town in chapter 01’s photograph of a public meeting?

rules.title: Use a district map to show one state’s races on the shapes of its districts, with party told by panel.
rule: Draw the state’s districts twice, one panel for each party, named with the seats it won: a district fills in its winner’s panel and shows as a thin gray outline in the other, so position carries party and no color does (Rule 14.7). Shade the winner’s margin in four gray steps, closer races lighter, the lightest with an edge, with the same steps and key words as the district tile map. Number each district on its shape, or beside it with a leader, and set the national result beside the panels.

text: Shapes let a reader find the district where they live, and two panels put each party’s seats together without a party color. Gray steps for the margin keep a close race and a safe one apart on both sides alike.

rules.builders: Form district-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s80; encode district, party and cls (the margin’s class from clerk-house-results-2024-classes, the table S82 reads); labels.layer the state’s fitted district layer (cd119-mi), labels.fips its code, labels.panels each party’s panel.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how close each race was in one state, and the districts’ shapes and places matter.

use_instead.when: Every seat in the country, each the same size
The reader looks up one race’s figures

correct.caption: How close was each of Michigan’s 2024 House races, by one margin rule for every kind of seat?

rules.title: Use a county choropleth for a pattern across thousands of places, and rank none of them.
rule: Shade every county by its class in four sequential steps, with no county lines, the state lines thin and gray, and a county with no estimate unshaded with an edge, named in a note. Set classes wide against the typical county’s margin of error, and say in a note what share of counties could fall in the next class, so the map reads as a pattern (Rule 14.9). Name no county in words unless its gap passes its margin. Put the national figure above the map, group the table by state and give every county with its margin in the download.

text: Counties show the pattern inside the states, such as cities against their rural neighbors. Small counties carry wide margins, so a county map answers “where” in broad strokes and leaves exact figures to the table.

rules.builders: Form county-choropleth: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s81; encode id (the geoid, in the layer’s order) and cls (each county’s class, written by a derive script so the page carries one small number a county); table.group groups the table by state, and the CSV export lists every county.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a figure varies across the whole country, place by place, and the pattern matters more than any one county.

use_instead.when: A figure by state
A count, such as jobs, where people or work cluster

correct.caption: How does median household income vary from county to county?

rules.title: Use a district tile map to show every House seat as one square, with party told by panel.
rule: Give each district one square of the same size on a layout that keeps states in their places and districts in their order, with lines between states and each state’s code where its block leaves room. Draw the map twice, one panel for each party, named with its seats, each seat filled in its winner’s panel and outlined in the other (Rule 14.7). Shade the margin in four gray steps, mark a seat unopposed on the ballot with a dot and a race decided another way with a ring, and name those seats in a note where the squares grow too small for the marks.

text: On a map of real districts, a few large rural seats fill the page while dozens of city seats shrink to dots. Equal squares give every seat the weight it has in the House, and the panels show each party’s seats without a party color.

rules.builders: Form district-tile-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s82; encode state, district, party, cls, mark, col and row, all in clerk-house-results-2024-classes, which cartographer_round3_derive.py writes from the Clerk’s results and our own tile layout built from the Census Bureau’s district centers; table.group groups the table by state.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which party won each House seat and by how much, and every seat should count the same.

use_instead.when: One state’s districts on their real shapes
How far each state moved, with direction

correct.caption: Which party won each House seat in 2024, and by how much, with the same margin classes as Michigan’s district map?

rules.title: Use a dot density map to show where a count clusters, each dot a stated number.
rule: Place one dot for each stated count, such as 10,000 employees, at random inside its county from a seed the chart records, and say that a dot is a count, never an address. Draw the dots in the subject ink over the land with thin gray state lines, raise the count per dot on a phone so the dots never cover the land, print the count in the key at every width, and say in a note how many units draw no dot (Rule 14.12).

text: A dot for every 10,000 shows both how many and where, so a crowded city and an empty county read for what they are. Random places inside each county keep a dot from pointing at any one address.

rules.builders: Form dot-density-map: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s83; encode id, dots and dots_phone (each county’s dots at the desk’s and the phone’s unit, from a derive script); labels.seed records the seed, labels.per the two units and labels.key the key’s words; the kit draws every dot as one path.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where people, jobs or homes are, and a count matters more than a rate.

use_instead.when: A rate, such as a share of households
A count by state, sized as circles

correct.caption: Where are the private-sector jobs?

rules.title: Use small-multiple maps to show how a pattern changed across a few dates, one map each.
rule: Draw the same map at each date, two to a row, in the same classes, inks and key, and name each panel with its date and its counts. Keep to a few dates spaced at a stated interval, all on one as-of day, and keep a period whole (Rule 14.10). Leave codes off the small panels and let the table give each state’s figure at each date.

text: Side by side, the same map at four dates shows a spread a reader can follow from one panel to the next. Counts under each panel give the change in numbers as well as in shade.

rules.builders: Form small-multiple-maps: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s84; encode code, panel (the date column) and category; labels.categories sets each class’s words in the key’s order, labels.panel_title and panel_counts each panel’s name and counts.
rules.use_when: The reader asks when and where something spread, such as states raising their minimum wage above the federal floor.

use_instead.when: One date, on a larger map
How far each state moved between two dates
The count over every year, as a line

correct.caption: When did states set their minimum wage above the federal $7.25?

rules.title: Avoid coloring a map by party, which takes a side before the reader reads it.
rule: Leave party colors, and above all red and blue, off every Oath & Action map, and draw no scale that runs from one party’s color to the other’s. Show who won by position and words: one panel for each party, named with the seats it won, each place filled in its winner’s panel and outlined in the other, and the margin in gray steps that darken as it widens (Rule 14.7). Show a shift with arrows and the direction named in words.

text: Red and blue are the parties’ own colors, so a map in them reads as one side’s scoreboard before anyone reads a number. On real shapes the color also lets land stand in for votes, and a party that wins large, thinly settled places looks bigger than its count.

rules.builders: No kit form, by design; draw district-map (s80) or district-tile-map (s82): labels.panels names each party with its seats, and the margin takes the gray magnitude steps.
rules.sketch_alt: The same invented results drawn twice: shaded from one party’s color to the other’s, the map takes a side at a glance, while two gray panels, one for each party’s seats, show who won each place and by how much with no color for either party.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks which party won each place, and by how much, gets a fairer answer from gray panels by party.

use_instead.when: Every House seat, who won it and by how much
One state’s districts on their real shapes
How far each state moved between two elections

correct.caption: The same invented results drawn twice: shaded from one party’s color to the other’s, the map takes a side at a glance, while two gray panels, one for each party’s seats, show who won each place and by how much with no color for either party.
correct.label: Party-colored map or red and blue scale, a form that misleads

rules.title: Set results as a table with each row’s margin drawn in it.
rule: Give each place one row: the later margin with the leader named in words, a bar from the center line toward the leader’s side, the earlier margin in gray and the shift as an arrow, all in neutral inks (Rule 14.7). Set the national row above the places, apart and labeled, and tag each row whose leader changed.
On a phone, where a full row does not fit, each row becomes a card that names the leader and margin in each year and gives the shift beside its arrow (Rule 14.12).

text: A table lets a reader find their own state by name and read its exact margin, which a map hides in its smallest places. The bar and arrow drawn in each row let the eye compare rows down the page without leaving the table.

rules.builders: Form results-table: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s15, or copy specs/s15.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.lead names each side’s party in words.
rules.use_when: The reader looks up how one place voted and how far it moved since the last election, among every state.

use_instead.when: The reader asks which places moved and how far, more than how each one voted
Where the places sit matters, so the shape of the country helps the reader
The rows are names and amounts a reader scans by rank

correct.caption: How did each state vote in 2024, and how did that compare with 2020?

rules.title: Rank a long list as a register a reader can scan.
rule: Give each item a row with its rank, its name with a short second line such as its kind, and its amount right-aligned in figures of one width, under column heads that carry the unit. Add a thin bar from zero for each amount so the drop down the list shows, keep hairlines between rows, and print the item the title names bold.
Keep names as the source gives them in the table, and say in a note when the drawing sets them differently.

text: A register keeps the name and the number side by side, which is what a reader looking for one group needs, and the rank tells them where it stands without counting. The thin bars add the shape of the drop from first to last at little cost in ink.

rules.builders: Form ranked-register: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s36, or copy specs/s36.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.divide, prefix and suffix set how each amount prints.
rules.use_when: The reader asks who leads a list of a dozen or more and wants to find a name and read its exact amount, such as the largest independent spenders in an election.

use_instead.when: The reader compares sizes more than reading names, among a dozen items or fewer
A handful of values to look up, with no ranking
The list is long enough that a reader needs to filter it
Each row is a claim with its grade, source and limits

correct.caption: Which groups spent the most on their own in the 2024 federal elections?

rules.title: Lay options against criteria in a matrix of the source’s own words.
rule: Put each option in a row and each criterion in a column, and print the source’s own words in every cell, so a reader compares options one criterion at a time. Leave out totals, counts and badges, since no one can add cells written in words. On a phone each row becomes a card that lists its columns (Rule 14.12).
The specimen also marks each cell with Oath & Action’s reading as a glyph and a tint, labeled as ours, the scenario view of Rule 14.76; a plain matrix prints the words alone.

text: A matrix holds every option against every criterion in one view, so a reader can read across a row or down a column. The source’s words keep its qualifiers, such as “slightly up in metro areas that reform housing rules”, which a score would throw away.

rules.builders: Form comparison-matrix: copy specs/s06.json, set form to comparison-matrix and point it at a new dataset; it prints the words alone, and scenario-directions adds the glyphs and tints.
rules.use_when: The reader weighs a few options across the same criteria, and the source describes each cell in words that do not reduce to a number.

use_instead.when: Every cell is a number and its size matters
The options are scenarios and each outcome has a direction
Two or three options read best as cards side by side

rules.title: Put a small trend line beside each row’s latest figures.
rule: Give each series one row: its name, a sparkline of its whole run with the end marked, and the latest figures in columns at the right. Draw every row’s sparkline on one shared scale, name the period once in the measure line, and print a peak the title or a note cites beside its point.

text: A sparkline gives a series’ path in the space of a word, so the table stays a table while the reader sees whether a figure came from a steady climb or a late turn. One shared scale keeps a flat line flat in every row.

rules.builders: Form sparkline-table: S13 draws it as its totals rows above the panels (node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s13); for a table alone, copy specs/s13.json, set form to sparkline-table and list the printed columns in encode.columns.
rules.use_when: The reader looks up a handful of series, such as all jobs and its parts, and wants each one’s latest figure with a sense of how it got there.

use_instead.when: The shape of each series matters more than its latest figure
One series, where each month’s value matters
The reader needs the figures alone, with no path

rules.title: Tint a grid of many cells by step, and print each cell’s word.
rule: Set rows down the left and columns across, tint each filled cell by its step on one ordered scale, light for the lowest and dark for the highest, and print the step’s word in every cell so the table reads in gray print and to a screen reader. Leave the cells unsummed, with no score or total, and mark a cell that carries a date or a caveat with a dot the key explains. Gather the rows under each group once, set every column’s head on one row over its own column, and frame the column the title names with its head in bold. Say in the table’s notes what a blank cell means.
Where a cell’s word cannot fit its column, as on a phone, each row becomes its name with a run of tinted chips that name the column and the word (Rule 14.12).

text: Tints let the eye find the dark and light patches across a grid of a hundred cells before reading any of them, and the printed word keeps every cell exact. One scale from light to dark reads as more and less in color, in gray print and for readers who see color differently.

rules.builders: Form heat-table: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s37, or copy specs/s37.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.steps orders the scale, labels.columns the columns and their heads’ lines, labels.groups the groups and labels.named the framed column.
rules.use_when: The reader looks across dozens of rows and several columns for a pattern, such as which routes the atlas rates feasible for which reforms, and each cell holds one rating or a small number.

use_instead.when: The cells hold the source’s own words, which no scale can order
Each cell is a value that changes over time and the trend matters
The grid is a map of places

correct.caption: Which routes could carry each reform, and how feasible is each?

rules.title: Let readers search and filter a long register, and count what matches.
rule: Print the register as a live table (Rule 18.10) under a labeled search field (Rule 18.15) and a Filters button with chips for each facet (Rule 18.16). Every keystroke or chip updates the rows at once, and one status line under the controls gives the count, such as “8 of 17 issue records”, with advice when nothing matches. With scripts off, the controls stay hidden and the whole table prints.
For a post or an email, print a still image of the register with one filter on, under the count line the live table would show.

text: A register of a hundred records answers a hundred questions, and a reader with one question needs a way in. A search and a few filters cut the table to the rows that answer it, and the count tells every reader, screen reader users among them, how many rows remain.

rules.builders: Form filterable-lookup-table: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s38, or copy specs/s38.json and point it at a new dataset; the spec’s lookup key names the searched columns and the filters, and labels.still the filter the still image shows.
rules.use_when: The reader comes with a question of their own and needs to find the few records that answer it in a register of dozens or hundreds, on the atlas site or in a report.

use_instead.when: The list is short enough to scan by rank
Each row is a claim the reader weighs, with its grade and limits
The piece is a post, an email or a social card, where a reader cannot click anything

correct.caption: Which issue records cover my question?

rules.title: Set claims beside their grade, period, coverage and limits.
rule: Give each claim one row in the source’s own words, with its grade in words and its period at the left, and who it covers, its source and its limits under it, each after a short head. Keep a claim’s limits in the same row as the claim, so no reader can quote one without the other, and say once in a note what each grade means (Rule 13.3).

text: A claim read apart from its grade and limits can say more than its evidence does. Setting them in one row means the qualification travels with the claim when a reader scans, quotes or shares it.

rules.builders: Form evidence-table: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s39, or copy specs/s39.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.grades prints each grade’s word and labels.heads the short heads.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what the evidence says on a subject and how far to trust each piece of it, as when weighing claims about drug prices.

use_instead.when: The reader asks how sure a whole body of evidence is, more than what each claim says
A few figures from one source answer the question
The reader weighs options against the same criteria in words

correct.caption: What does the evidence say about drug middlemen and prices?

rules.title: List tracked bills with their six steps, status and date.
rule: Draw each bill as chapter 11 draws a list of bills (Rule 11.5): its number and name lead the row, its six numbered steps run across, and its status follows in words with the date of the latest action. A bill that became law fills all six steps and says so with its date and law number (Rule 11.3). Give the date Oath & Action checked the whole list in the title or measure line, since a tracker shows one day.

text: A reader tracking bills wants the same answer for each one: how far it has come, what happened last and when. The six marks answer the first at a glance, in the same shapes the reader meets on every Oath & Action tracker, and the dated words answer the rest.

rules.builders: Form tracker-list: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s40, or copy specs/s40.json and point it at a new dataset; encode.step and encode.skipped give each bill’s steps, labels.steps their names.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where a set of bills or rules stands today, and what has happened to each, for the Track pillar.

use_instead.when: One bill’s full path with every date, on its own page
When each part of one law takes effect
How many items sit at each stage, with no single bill named

correct.caption: Where do the housing bills of this Congress stand?

rules.title: Set a handful of numbers as a plain table when a chart adds nothing.
rule: Set the numbers in rows under short column heads, with each row’s name at the left and its values right-aligned in figures of one width, a hairline under the heads and a rule under the last row. Keep the table only as wide as its columns need, and print it with its title, measure line, notes and source line like any chart (Rule 14.2).

text: Three numbers within two points of each other make bars of almost the same length, which tells the reader less than the figures do. A table puts the exact value where the eye lands, keeps live text for screen readers and copying, and costs the page almost nothing.

rules.builders: Form plain-table: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s41, or copy specs/s41.json and point it at a new dataset; encode.columns lists the value columns in order.
rules.use_when: The reader wants to look up a few exact values, such as three survey shares, and their sizes are close enough that bars would only repeat the numbers.

use_instead.when: One finding answers the question and a sentence states it faster
The reader compares sizes across a dozen or more rows
A long list needs sorting and scanning by rank
Each row also carries a trend the reader should see

correct.caption: Do Republicans and Democrats agree on a ban on stock trading by members of Congress?

rules.title: Write one sourced sentence when it answers faster than a chart.
rule: When one or two figures answer the reader’s question, state them in one sentence with the figures, the period, whom the survey counted and the grade’s verb, and print the full source line under it (Rule 13.6). The sentence keeps its evidence label, and its figures stay in a table under it for anyone who wants them in rows (Rule 14.13).

text: Two numbers of almost the same size make a chart of two equal shapes, which says less than the numbers do. A sentence names whom the survey counted and when in the same breath as the figures, so a reader can quote it whole with its source.

rules.builders: Form one-sentence: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s42; labels.sentence carries the sentence, and show leaves out the printed title so it appears once.
rules.use_when: The answer is one finding of one or two figures, such as how many voters in each party favored a ban, and a reader would take longer to read a chart than the sentence.

use_instead.when: A reader will want to look up three or more exact values
One figure leads and its context matters, such as a share with the votes that followed it
The figures differ in size and the difference is the point

correct.caption: Do Republicans and Democrats agree on a ban on stock trading by members of Congress? One sourced sentence answers.
